nodes.text: Painless oral ulcers, cytopenias, and nephritis with anti-dsDNA suggest systemic lupus erythematosus.
Check ANA, CBC, creatinine, urinalysis, urine protein-to-creatinine ratio, and complement.
**ANA positive with compatible clinical features:** check anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm.
**Reactive RPR:** confirm with a treponemal test because lupus can cause a biologic false-positive RPR.
**Protein-to-creatinine ratio >0.5 g/g or unexplained renal dysfunction:** arrange kidney biopsy.
Use hydroxychloroquine unless contraindicated and monitor renal findings, complement, and anti-dsDNA.
**Organ-threatening disease:** give IV methylprednisolone and tailor immunosuppression to organ involvement and renal biopsy class.
**Active proliferative nephritis:** consider mycophenolate-based combination therapy with belimumab or a calcineurin inhibitor.

algorithm.title: Sample size, power, and statistical errors

nodes.text: Hypothesis testing: establish null hypothesis (H0) vs alternative hypothesis (H1)

**Increasing sample size (N):** enhances study power, directly decreasing beta (type II error)
Determinants of required sample size: alpha level + desired power + expected effect size + population variance

f120-2019-q064.trap: Recurrent bruises and falls tempt suspected child abuse or age-appropriate behavior, but severe pervasive hyperactivity across school and home identifies ADHD.

A.fit: Here: classroom hyperactivity, dislocated shoulder, multiple fall injuries

B.fit: Not here: high activity and accidental injuries without antisocial aggression

C.fit: Not here: primary motor hyperactivity and physical impulsivity across settings

nodes.text: Inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity: >= 6 symptoms present for >= 6 months in >= 2 settings before age 12
Standardized rating scales: obtain Vanderbilt or Conners assessments from both parents and teachers
**Preschool children (age 4-5 years):** first-line therapy is behavioral parent training and classroom interventions
**School-age children (age >= 6 years):** first-line therapy is stimulant medication (methylphenidate) + behavioral therapy
**Substance use concern or intolerable stimulant side effects:** non-stimulant options (atomoxetine, guanfacine)
Monitor therapy: track blood pressure, pulse, growth curve, and academic progress at regular follow-up visits

nodes.text: Glucose ≥ 200, ketones ≥ 3 mmol/L, pH < 7.3 or HCO3 < 18: DKA
IV isotonic crystalloid first
**K < 3.5 mEq/L:** replace potassium; delay insulin
**K 3.5–5.0 mEq/L:** add potassium to fluids; start insulin
Continuous IV regular insulin infusion
**Glucose < 250 mg/dL:** add dextrose; continue insulin until ketoacidosis resolves
**pH < 7.0:** consider bicarbonate
Resolved: ketones < 0.6 mmol/L and pH ≥ 7.3 or HCO3 ≥ 18; overlap SC basal insulin

Perform endometrial biopsy for bleeding with obesity, chronic unopposed estrogen, or age ≥45.
**Postmenopausal bleeding with cancer risk factors or recurrent bleeding:** obtain transvaginal ultrasound and endometrial sampling.
**Hyperplasia without atypia:** use levonorgestrel IUD or oral progestin.
**Atypical hyperplasia:** refer for total hysterectomy.
**Endometrial carcinoma:** refer to gynecologic oncology for surgical staging.
Use transvaginal ultrasound or sonohysterography to assess for fibroids and polyps.

**A1c ≥8.5% without acidosis:** start basal insulin while initiating metformin.
**Ketoacidosis:** start IV fluids and potassium-guided IV insulin.

f120-2019-q068.hinge: Connective tissue disorder with joint hypermobility, apical click (MVP), and family history of aortic dissection requires echocardiography to assess aortic root dilation.

C.fit: Not here: cardiac evaluation takes priority given family aortic rupture

E.clue: Invasive catheterization visualizing aortic lumen
E.fit: Not here: non-invasive echocardiography is the initial diagnostic modality of choice

algorithm.title: Connective tissue disorders and aortic root dilation (Marfan / EDS)

nodes.text: Marfanoid habitus, joint hypermobility, or family history of premature aortic aneurysm: suspect connective tissue disorder
Initial cardiac evaluation: perform transthoracic echocardiography to measure aortic root diameter and detect mitral valve prolapse
**Aortic root z-score >= 2 or progressive dilation:** initiate prophylactic beta-blocker (atenolol) or ARB (losartan)
**Severe aortic root enlargement (diameter >= 50 mm):** elective prophylactic aortic root replacement surgery
Serial monitoring: repeat annual echocardiography to track aortic dimensions and valvular regurgitation
Activity restrictions: avoid competitive collision sports, heavy weightlifting, and isometric straining

f120-2019-q069.boardCall: Episodic vertigo lasting hours + sensorineural hearing loss + tinnitus + aural fullness -> Meniere's disease (Endolymphatic hydrops)
f120-2019-q069.hinge: Recurrent episodes of rotatory vertigo lasting hours accompanied by fluctuating unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness define Ménière disease.
f120-2019-q069.trap: Episodic vertigo tempts BPPV, but BPPV lasts seconds, is triggered by head movements, and lacks hearing loss, tinnitus, or aural fullness.

B.fit: Not here: episodes last 12 hours with hearing loss and tinnitus

C.fit: Not here: 12-hour ear-specific triad without focal neurologic deficits

D.clue: Endolymphatic hydrops causing episodic vertigo and tinnitus
D.fit: Here: 12-hour vertigo attacks, tinnitus, aural fullness, right hearing loss

E.clue: Single acute vertigo episode after viral infection
E.fit: Not here: recurrent separate 12-hour episodes over 3 months

nodes.text: Recurrent vertigo episodes (20 min to 12 hours) + low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss + tinnitus + aural fullness: Ménière disease
Audiometric testing: document fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss in affected ear
Acute attack therapy: vestibular suppressants (meclizine) and antiemetics (ondansetron)
Maintenance prevention: dietary restriction of salt (< 2 g/day), caffeine, and alcohol + thiazide diuretic
**Refractory disabling vertigo despite medical therapy:** intratympanic gentamicin or corticosteroid injections
**Intractable vertigo with profound non-serviceable hearing loss:** surgical labyrinthectomy or vestibular neurectomy

f120-2019-q070.hinge: Severe heat exhaustion with hypovolemic hypotension (90/65 mm Hg) and vomiting requires immediate intravenous fluid resuscitation.

nodes.text: Exertional heat illness with vomiting and hypotension suggests clinically significant volume depletion.
Give IV isotonic crystalloid for hypovolemic hypotension.
Remove excess clothing and move to a cool area; check rectal temperature.
**Altered mental status with exertional hyperthermia:** start immediate cold-water immersion for heat stroke.
**Rhabdomyolysis:** give isotonic fluids and trend creatinine, potassium, and urine output.
**Evolving coagulopathy or multiorgan dysfunction:** admit to intensive care.

B.fit: Not here: direct bilirubin is normal at 0.2 mg/dL

C.fit: Not here: predominantly conjugated hyperbilirubinemia seen in Rotor

D.clue: Impaired organic anion transporter uptake into hepatocytes
D.fit: Not here: primary pathophysiology in Gilbert is deficient conjugation

nodes.text: Isolated elevated bilirubin with direct fraction < 20%: confirm unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia
Decreased conjugation of bilirubin via reduced UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity: Gilbert syndrome
**Rule out hemolysis:** check CBC, reticulocyte count, haptoglobin, and peripheral smear
**Normal transaminases, normal alkaline phosphatase, and no hemolysis:** establish Gilbert syndrome
Precipitating triggers: mild jaundice typically recurs during fasting, illness, physical exertion, or stress
Definitive management: patient reassurance regarding benign prognosis; no pharmacologic treatment or liver biopsy indicated

nodes.text: Opening snap + apical diastolic rumble + rheumatic history → mitral stenosis; TTE
Echo: valve area (severe ≤ 1.5 cm²), mean gradient, Wilkins score

**Symptomatic, area ≤ 1.5 cm², pliable valve, no LA thrombus:** balloon commissurotomy
**Heavy calcification, LA thrombus on TEE or ≥ moderate MR:** surgical mitral valve replacement
**Pulmonary edema:** diuretics + heart rate slowing to lengthen diastole
Secondary prophylaxis: IM benzathine penicillin G

nodes.text: Neural tube closure occurs early, often before pregnancy is recognized.
Start folic acid at least one month before conception and continue through the first trimester.

**Enzyme-inducing antiseizure medication:** review the regimen and individualize folic acid with the treating clinicians.
**Vegan diet:** assess vitamin B12 intake and supplement when needed.

nodes.text: Advanced cancer + persistent crying, hopelessness, or withdrawal: evaluate for major depressive disorder
Immediate essential safety step: assess for suicidal ideation, intent, plan, and means
**Active suicidal intent or plan present:** emergency psychiatric evaluation + continuous 1-on-1 observation
Rule out organic drivers: check pain control, delirium, hypercalcemia, and medication side effects
**Confirmed depression with prognosis of weeks:** low-dose psychostimulant (methylphenidate) for rapid mood enhancement
**Confirmed depression with prognosis of months:** optimize SSRI (adjust fluoxetine) or add mirtazapine

abdominal-trauma.name: Abdominal trauma
abdominal-trauma.scope: Blunt abdominal trauma (splenic/hepatic laceration, FAST exam, CT scan), penetrating abdominal trauma (stab, gunshot, peritonitis, exploratory laparotomy indications)
abdominal-trauma.core: Abdominal injury after collision, fall, stabbing, or gunshot: hemodynamic status and peritoneal signs determine imaging versus immediate operation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: High-speed deceleration, seat-belt compression, lower rib fractures; anticoagulation increases bleeding risk
Stab wounds may spare viscera; bullets frequently injure multiple structures

rows.label: Clues
items: LUQ pain or referred left shoulder pain → splenic injury; RUQ tenderness → hepatic injury
Distention, ecchymoses, abdominal wall marks; initially benign examination does not exclude bowel injury
★ **Rigidity, rebound, persistent hypotension**, or evisceration → urgent operative assessment

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Solid-organ disruption → intraperitoneal hemorrhage; mesenteric injury → ischemia or delayed perforation
Retroperitoneal injury may produce little intraperitoneal free fluid

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **FAST** at bedside during resuscitation; detects free fluid, not organ-specific injury
★ Stable → **CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast**; evaluate solid organs, bowel, retroperitoneum
Negative FAST with ongoing shock → search thorax/pelvis, repeat assessment; do not assume safety
Stable anterior stab → local wound exploration or serial examination/CT; trajectory guides evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: Airway, large-bore IV access, warmed blood products; massive transfusion for hemorrhagic shock
★ Unstable + positive FAST, peritonitis, or ongoing transfusion need → **exploratory laparotomy**; no CT delay
Stable splenic/hepatic injury → monitored nonoperative care; blush, transient response → angioembolization (older questions: laparotomy)
Enteric contents, uncontrolled bleeding → operation; transperitoneal gunshot → **laparotomy** even if stable; selected stabs observed
Suspected bowel perforation → ceftriaxone + metronidazole, trauma surgery; free subdiaphragmatic air → **laparotomy**, no CT

rows.label: Complications
items: Delayed splenic rupture, abscess, bile leak, abdominal compartment syndrome
Missed hollow-viscus injury → sepsis; splenectomy → overwhelming encapsulated bacterial infection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Restraints, airbags, injury-prevention counseling
★ After splenectomy → **pneumococcal, meningococcal, Hib vaccines**; fever requires urgent antibiotics

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pelvic hemorrhage: unstable pelvis, negative abdominal FAST
Tension pneumothorax: unilateral absent breath sounds, obstructive shock

abdominal-trauma.evidence: Not checked online; established trauma assessment and management principles.

abnormal-uterine-bleeding.name: Abnormal uterine bleeding
abnormal-uterine-bleeding.scope: Adenomyosis, leiomyomas, endometrial polyps, ovulatory dysfunction, PALM-COEIN classification, endometrial biopsy
abnormal-uterine-bleeding.core: Abnormal uterine bleeding requires pregnancy exclusion, hemodynamic assessment and evaluation for structural disease or unopposed endometrial estrogen.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Perimenopause, PCOS, obesity, anticoagulants; lifelong heavy bleeding suggests inherited coagulopathy
Adenomyosis often multiparous; fibroids common during reproductive years

rows.label: Clues
items: Bleeding affecting quality of life, prolonged/heavy menses, intermenstrual or irregular bleeding
Tachycardia, orthostasis or syncope → clinically important blood loss
Postmenopausal bleeding requires malignancy evaluation even with a single episode

rows.label: Pathophys
items: PALM: Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Malignancy/hyperplasia → structural causes
COEIN: Coagulopathy, Ovulatory dysfunction, Endometrial, Iatrogenic, Not otherwise classified
Anovulation → absent cyclic progesterone, unopposed proliferation and unstable shedding
Combined OCPs → uniform estrogen/progestin exposure **synchronizes endometrium**, preventing irregular shedding

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Pregnancy test and CBC** first; pelvic examination localizes uterine versus cervical/vaginal bleeding
**Transvaginal ultrasound** evaluates structural lesions; saline sonohysterography/hysteroscopy for intracavitary disease
★ **Endometrial biopsy ≥45 years**; younger with persistent bleeding, unopposed estrogen or failed treatment
Postmenopausal bleeding: endometrial thickness >4 mm → sampling; persistent bleeding → biopsy regardless of thickness
TSH for suspected endocrine disease; coagulation/vWF testing for suggestive bleeding history

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Unstable → IV access, blood resuscitation, urgent gynecology; tamponade or operative control if needed
Stable → high-dose combined OCP, progestin, tranexamic acid; no estrogen if prior VTE, hypertension, smoker >35
★ Long-term → **levonorgestrel IUD**, OCP/progestin; family complete, normal cavity → **ablation**; copper worsens
Fibroids: asymptomatic → **observation, any size**; symptomatic → myomectomy/embolization; hysterectomy if childbearing done
Polyp → hysteroscopic removal; adenomyosis refractory to hormones → hysterectomy

rows.label: Complications
items: Iron deficiency anemia; chronic anovulation → endometrial hyperplasia/cancer; structural lesions can impair fertility

rows.label: Prevention
items: Regular progestin exposure for chronic anovulation; replace iron and address metabolic drivers

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pregnancy complication: positive hCG; exclude ectopic pregnancy
Cervicitis: friable cervix and postcoital bleeding

table.title: Cause clues
rows: Firm irregular enlarged uterus; pressure symptoms
Labor-like pain, dilated os, beefy prolapsing tissue
Tender uterus; biopsy **plasma cells**, not neutrophils

acid-base-disorders.name: Acid-base disorders
acid-base-disorders.scope: Metabolic acidosis (anion gap, non-anion gap), metabolic alkalosis (saline-responsive vs saline-resistant), respiratory acidosis, respiratory alkalosis, Winter formula, mixed disorders
acid-base-disorders.core: Identify the primary pH disturbance, test expected compensation, then investigate the anion gap or urine chloride to locate the cause.

rows.label: Definition
items: Acidemia: pH <7.35; alkalemia: >7.45; normal pH can hide opposing primary disorders
Metabolic: primary HCO3 change; respiratory: primary PaCO2 change

rows.label: Formula
items: ★ **AG = Na − (Cl + HCO3)**; usual normal ≈8–12, laboratory dependent
Hypoalbuminemia correction: add 2.5 to AG per 1 g/dL albumin below 4
★ **Winter: expected PaCO2 = 1.5 × HCO3 + 8 ±2**

rows.label: Interpret
items: HCO3 12 → expected PaCO2 26 ±2; measured 40 → additional respiratory acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis: expected PaCO2 ≈40 + 0.7 × (HCO3 − 24), ±5
Respiratory HCO3 change per 10 PaCO2: acidosis +1 acute/+4 chronic; alkalosis −2 acute/−4 chronic

rows.label: Use when
items: ★ Alkalosis: **urine Cl <20 mmol/L** → saline-responsive; ≥20 → diuretics/mineralocorticoids
ΔAG exceeds HCO3 fall → additional alkalosis; smaller ΔAG → additional non-gap acidosis

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Compensation never overshoots; values outside expected range imply **mixed disorder**
Salicylates often cause respiratory alkalosis plus high-gap acidosis; near-normal pH is deceptive
Diarrhea/RTA: non-gap acidosis; distal RTA: urine pH >5.5, hypokalemia; renal failure: either gap pattern

acid-base-disorders.evidence: Established physiologic formulas; no guideline involved.

acute-kidney-injury.name: Acute kidney injury
acute-kidney-injury.core: Abrupt loss of renal filtration: separate impaired perfusion, parenchymal injury, and urinary obstruction before treating the cause.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Volume depletion, sepsis, cirrhosis, low-output heart failure (prerenal despite overload); baseline CKD increases vulnerability
NSAIDs constrict afferent arterioles; ACE inhibitors/ARBs reduce efferent tone during hypoperfusion
Aminoglycosides, pigment (dipstick blood, few RBCs), prolonged ischemia → tubular damage; antibiotics/PPIs → tubulointerstitial inflammation

rows.label: Clues
items: Oliguria, edema, uremic nausea; urine output may remain normal
AIN: fever, rash, eosinophilia sometimes present; classic triad often absent
★ Pulmonary edema, severe hyperkalemia, encephalopathy, pericarditis → **urgent renal support**
Anuria despite patent catheter after pelvic surgery + hydronephrosis → ureteral injury/ligation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Reduced glomerular pressure, tubular epithelial injury, or backpressure → declining GFR

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ AKI: creatinine ↑≥0.3 mg/dL within 48 h, ≥1.5-fold within 7 days, or oliguria
Oliguria criterion: urine <0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥6 h; trend creatinine, electrolytes, fluid balance
★ **Urinalysis + microscopy**, medication review; bladder scan → renal ultrasound if obstruction possible
FeNa unreliable with diuretics, CKD, early obstruction; urine eosinophils neither sensitive nor specific
Unexplained persistent injury or suspected glomerulonephritis → nephrology, possible kidney biopsy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe hyperkalemia → **IV calcium**, insulin/dextrose; refractory electrolyte disturbance → dialysis
Hypovolemia (postoperative oliguria, high urine specific gravity) → saline bolus; congestion → loop diuretic; no reflex fluids in overload
Stop nephrotoxins, all NSAIDs including celecoxib (intra-articular steroid for joint pain); persistent AIN → glucocorticoids; renal-dose drugs
★ Obstruction → **catheter or ureteral decompression**; monitor postobstructive diuresis
Dialysis: refractory acidosis, hyperkalemia, intoxication, overload, symptomatic uremia; no isolated creatinine threshold

rows.label: Complications
items: Arrhythmias, acidosis, volume overload; subsequent CKD
Recovery diuresis → dehydration and electrolyte losses

rows.label: Prevention
items: Maintain perfusion during illness; review nephrotoxic combinations and monitor renal function
Contrast in high-risk CKD → **periprocedural IV isotonic saline**; diuretics, mannitol, metformin stop don't protect
ACR now limits contrast prophylaxis mainly to eGFR <30; older exam questions may expect wider hydration

rows.label: Mimics
items: CKD: longstanding abnormalities, small echogenic kidneys, chronic anemia
Trimethoprim effect: creatinine rise without true GFR decline

acute-kidney-injury.evidence: Not checked online; established KDIGO diagnostic criteria and renal teaching.

acute-otitis-media.name: Acute otitis media
acute-otitis-media.scope: Bulging erythematous tympanic membrane, impaired mobility, oral amoxicillin first-line, amoxicillin-clavulanate, tympanostomy indications
acute-otitis-media.core: Acute otalgia with middle-ear effusion and a bulging tympanic membrane identifies acute otitis media; age, laterality, and severity guide antibiotics.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Young age, daycare, viral URI, tobacco smoke exposure, absent breastfeeding
Craniofacial abnormalities and eustachian tube dysfunction increase recurrence

rows.label: Clues
items: Ear tugging, fever, irritability, poor feeding; spontaneous perforation causes new otorrhea
★ **Postauricular swelling/tenderness, protruding pinna** → mastoiditis
Erythematous membrane alone, especially during crying, insufficient for diagnosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: URI-related eustachian edema traps fluid; pneumococcus, nontypeable H influenzae, Moraxella commonly infect middle ear

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Pneumatic otoscopy**: reduced mobility supports effusion; moderate/severe bulging or nonexternal otorrhea diagnostic
Mild bulging requires recent otalgia or intense erythema; no effusion → no AOM diagnosis
Tympanometry if effusion uncertain; no routine imaging/cultures; suspected mastoiditis → **contrast CT temporal bones/head**
Failure after 48–72 h → repeat examination; persistent effusion alone does not mean antibiotic failure

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Acetaminophen or ibuprofen** for pain regardless of antibiotic decision
★ When treating → **amoxicillin 80–90 mg/kg/day**; 10 days if <2 years or severe
Recent amoxicillin within 30 days, purulent conjunctivitis, or amoxicillin failure → amoxicillin-clavulanate
Selected older nonsevere cases → 5–7 days; severe illness/complication or oral intolerance changes regimen
★ Recurrent AOM **≥3/6 months or ≥4/12 months** → tube evaluation; effusion required at candidacy assessment

rows.label: Complications
items: Conductive hearing loss, membrane perforation, mastoiditis, rare intracranial infection
Effusion ≥3 months → hearing assessment; tubes considered for bilateral persistent fluid with hearing difficulty

rows.label: Prevention
items: Pneumococcal/influenza vaccination, breastfeeding, smoke avoidance; no routine prophylactic antibiotics
Observe speech/hearing development in recurrent disease

rows.label: Mimics
items: Otitis media with effusion: fluid, retracted gray membrane, no acute inflammation → **observe, no antibiotics**
Otitis externa: canal inflammation, pain with tragus/pinna movement
Referred dental/TMJ pain: normal middle-ear examination

acute-rhinosinusitis.name: Acute rhinosinusitis
acute-rhinosinusitis.scope: Common cold, viral rhinosinusitis, acute bacterial rhinosinusitis criteria, symptomatic therapy, antibiotic stewardship
acute-rhinosinusitis.core: Acute nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, and facial pressure usually reflect a self-limited viral infection; duration and course identify likely bacterial disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Respiratory exposure, daycare contacts, impaired drainage from allergic inflammation
Immunocompromise, recent antibiotics, or hospitalization increases resistant-organism risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Cough, reduced smell, maxillary tenderness; colored mucus alone does not establish bacterial infection
★ Orbital swelling, painful eye movement, reduced vision, severe headache → **complicated infection**
Well febrile child, URI symptoms, clear lungs, good perfusion: soft flow murmur innocent, not VSD

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Viral mucosal edema blocks sinus drainage; secondary infection commonly pneumococcus, H influenzae, or Moraxella

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; uncomplicated illness needs neither sinus radiographs nor CT
Persistent, severe, or biphasic course identifies bacterial cases; fever alone is insufficient
Suspected orbital/intracranial extension → contrast CT; MRI for intracranial definition
Refractory or unusual infection → ENT evaluation; routine nasal swab cultures unhelpful

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Viral illness → **saline irrigation, acetaminophen/NSAID**, oral pseudoephedrine (not young children); no antibiotics
Intranasal fluticasone for associated allergic inflammation; topical oxymetazoline at most 3 days
★ Uncomplicated bacterial illness + reliable follow-up → **watchful waiting** or antibiotics
Antibiotic choice: amoxicillin-clavulanate, usually 5–7 days in adults; penicillin allergy → doxycycline
Complication → admission, IV ampicillin-sulbactam, urgent ENT/ophthalmology; avoid empiric azithromycin because resistance

rows.label: Complications
items: Orbital cellulitis or abscess, cavernous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, intracranial abscess
Unnecessary antibiotics → diarrhea, C difficile, resistance

rows.label: Prevention
items: Hand hygiene, smoking avoidance, control allergic rhinitis
Sterile/distilled or previously boiled water for nasal irrigation

rows.label: Mimics
items: Allergic rhinitis: itching, sneezing, watery discharge without fever
Migraine: episodic disabling headache, photophobia, nausea
Dental infection: focal tooth pain, unilateral maxillary symptoms

table.title: Bacterial patterns
rows: Initial improvement → new fever or worsening symptoms

adrenal-masses.name: Adrenal masses
adrenal-masses.scope: Adrenal incidentaloma, adrenocortical carcinoma, functional vs nonfunctional evaluation, pheochromocytoma, hyperaldosteronism, Cushing syndrome, hyperandrogenism (DHEA-S), adrenal CT imaging, adrenalectomy indications
adrenal-masses.core: An incidental adrenal lesion requires two decisions: malignant potential on imaging and clinically important hormone secretion.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Incidental detection increases with age; known extra-adrenal cancer raises metastatic risk
MEN2/VHL/NF1 predispose to pheochromocytoma; most incidental lesions are benign cortical adenomas

rows.label: Clues
items: Often asymptomatic; weight loss, flank pain, rapid growth, or mixed steroid excess suggest carcinoma
Episodic headache/palpitations/diaphoresis → catecholamines; proximal weakness/easy bruising → cortisol excess
Resistant hypertension/hypokalemia → aldosterone; rapid virilization → adrenal androgen secretion

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Cortical tumors may secrete cortisol, aldosterone, or androgens; medullary tumors secrete catecholamines
Autonomous cortisol suppresses ACTH and contralateral adrenal function

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Noncontrast adrenal CT** first; assess density, homogeneity, size, invasion; indeterminate → dedicated imaging
★ **1 mg overnight dexamethasone**: cortisol >1.8 µg/dL suggests autonomy; confirm ACTH independence
Plasma free or urinary fractionated metanephrines if lesion not clearly benign or pheochromocytoma symptoms
Hypertension/hypokalemia → aldosterone/renin; virilization/possible carcinoma → DHEA-S, precursors; **high DHEA-S** → adrenal source
★ **Never biopsy before excluding pheochromocytoma**; biopsy rarely distinguishes adenoma from cortical carcinoma

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Clinically significant unilateral hormone excess → **adrenalectomy**; suspected carcinoma requires preoperative staging
Pheochromocytoma: **phenoxybenzamine** alpha blockade, volume repletion before surgery; beta blockade only after alpha
Mild cortisol autonomy: individualize surgery by diabetes, hypertension, skeletal disease, and operative risk
Indeterminate unoperated lesion → repeat CT/MRI in 6–12 months; growth prompts reassessment

rows.label: Complications
items: Pheochromocytoma manipulation → hypertensive crisis; carcinoma → metastases
Postoperative adrenal insufficiency after cortisol-producing tumor removal → perioperative glucocorticoid coverage

rows.label: Prevention
items: Address cortisol-associated cardiometabolic and bone risk; genetic counseling for syndromic catecholamine tumors

rows.label: Mimics
items: Myelolipoma: macroscopic fat on CT
Adrenal metastasis: cancer history, often bilateral; biopsy only if management changes
Adrenal hemorrhage: acute pain, anticoagulation/trauma context, evolving imaging appearance

table.title: Imaging changes the answer
rows: Benign; no further imaging regardless of size

adult-immunizations.name: Adult immunizations
adult-immunizations.scope: Routine adult vaccines, immunocompromised and HIV, pregnancy, live-vaccine contraindications, chronic medical conditions (COPD, diabetes, liver disease), vaccine counseling and addressing hesitancy
adult-immunizations.core: Match vaccination to age, prior doses, pregnancy, immune status, and exposure risk; missed series resume without restarting.

rows.label: Who
items: ★ **HepB**: all 19–59; ≥60 with risk/request; health worker anti-HBs negative post-series → revaccinate
**HIV any CD4**, liver disease/alcohol, COPD, diabetes, smoking → pneumococcal <50; liver → HepA/HepB
Asplenia → pneumococcal, MenACWY, MenB, Hib; HIV → MenACWY

rows.label: Start/stop
items: ★ Pregnancy: **Tdap each pregnancy at 27–36 wk**; inactivated influenza any trimester
Maternal RSV: Abrysvo at 32–36 wk, September–January; previous pregnancy dose → infant antibody instead
RSV once: all ≥75; ages 50–74 with increased severe-disease risk

rows.label: Test
items: Anti-HBs/anti-HAV/VZV IgG positive → immune, skip; otherwise **do not delay vaccination** for serology
★ Immunocompromised ≥19 → recombinant zoster; HIV CD4 ≥200 permits MMR/varicella if nonimmune
HPV started <15 → two doses; ≥15 or immunocompromised → three

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **No live MMR, varicella, intranasal influenza**: severe immunosuppression, pregnancy (nonimmune → postpartum)
PCV15 → PPSV23: ≥8 weeks immunocompromised; older exams: PPSV23 alone; mild illness/antibiotics: no deferral
Hesitancy → elicit concern; inactivated influenza cannot cause flu, coincidental virus; refusal → document, revisit

table.title: Routine adult schedule
rows: Annual influenza; updated COVID-19 for all adults
Tdap once, then either every 10 years
PCV20/21 alone; PCV15 → PPSV23 after 1 year

alcohol-use-disorder.name: Alcohol use disorder
alcohol-use-disorder.scope: Unhealthy alcohol use, CAGE and AUDIT screening, transaminitis (AST > ALT), motivational interviewing, naltrexone, acamprosate
alcohol-use-disorder.core: Compulsive alcohol use despite harm, impaired control, or physiologic dependence calls for nonjudgmental assessment and relapse-prevention treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family history, early initiation, trauma, depression, anxiety, social stress
Binge drinking and escalating tolerance; coexisting sedative use increases overdose risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Craving, failed attempts to cut down, role impairment, continued use despite consequences
AST:ALT ≥1.5–2, macrocytosis, elevated GGT support exposure but neither prove nor exclude disorder
★ Tremor, tachycardia, hallucinations, seizures after reduction → **withdrawal**, potentially fatal

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Chronic GABA enhancement/NMDA inhibition → compensatory adaptation; cessation unmasks CNS excitation
Mesolimbic reinforcement and stress circuitry sustain compulsive use and relapse

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Screen adults using **AUDIT-C** or single-question heavy-use screen; positive result → fuller assessment
DSM-5: ≥2 of 11 criteria within 12 months; 2–3 mild, 4–5 moderate, ≥6 severe
CAGE: Cut down, Annoyed, Guilty, Eye-opener; ≥2 positive suggests problem use, misses early risky drinking
Assess suicidality, other drugs, liver disease, nutritional deficiency, pregnancy, withdrawal history
Depression or major life stressor → always ask about alcohol use

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Motivational interviewing**: elicit goals, reflect ambivalence, agree achievable change; CBT and mutual support
Withdrawal → benzodiazepines; inpatient detoxification for severe history, unstable comorbidity, or unreliable support
Thiamine promptly for malnutrition/Wernicke risk; never delay emergency glucose for hypoglycemia
Disulfiram: selected supervised abstinence; avoid severe liver/cardiac disease; alcohol exposure causes aversive reaction

rows.label: Complications
items: Cirrhosis, pancreatitis, cardiomyopathy, neuropathy, cancer, injuries, fetal alcohol effects
Wernicke encephalopathy → Korsakoff amnesia; depression and suicide risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Ongoing **relapse planning**, frequent follow-up, social support; abstinence for pregnancy or advanced liver disease
Assess hepatitis vaccination, nutrition, driving safety, medication interactions
Asymptomatic AST>ALT transaminitis (<500, unlike viral >1000) in daily drinker → reversible with abstinence

rows.label: Mimics
items: Sedative withdrawal: similar autonomic excitation with benzodiazepine/barbiturate reduction
Hyperthyroidism: tremor/tachycardia without alcohol-linked time course

table.title: Relapse prevention
rows: Current opioids; acute hepatitis/severe hepatic failure

alcohol-use-disorder.evidence: Not checked online; established screening and addiction-treatment principles.

alcohol-withdrawal.name: Alcohol withdrawal
alcohol-withdrawal.core: Autonomic and neuropsychiatric excitation after reducing prolonged heavy alcohol intake; progression from mild symptoms to life-threatening delirium.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior withdrawal seizures/delirium, repeated detoxifications, heavy sustained use, older age
Acute illness, electrolyte depletion, concurrent sedative dependence; poor support increases outpatient failure

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Diaphoresis, tachycardia, hypertension, insomnia, nausea; symptoms possible with **positive blood alcohol**
Hospital day 2–5 or postoperative: new agitation, hallucinations, autonomic signs → suspect **unreported alcohol use**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Chronic ethanol → downregulated GABA inhibition/upregulated NMDA excitation; cessation unmasks neuronal hyperactivity
Repeated episodes → kindling, progressively lower seizure threshold

rows.label: Dx
items: **Clinical diagnosis** + time since reduction; bedside glucose, CBC, electrolytes, Mg, phosphate, liver tests
★ **CIWA-Ar** if communicative; ≥19 severe; delirium/intubation → **RASS/MINDS**
First/focal seizure, head injury, focal deficit, atypical timing → head CT; do not assume withdrawal

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Diazepam/chlordiazepoxide** symptom-triggered; liver dysfunction/older frail adults → **lorazepam/oxazepam**
★ Seizures/delirium → monitored inpatient **IV benzodiazepines**; refractory → ICU phenobarbital with respiratory monitoring
★ **Parenteral thiamine**; hypoglycemia → immediate dextrose, never wait; correct electrolyte deficits
Phenytoin ineffective; dexmedetomidine adjunct; **chlorpromazine**/antipsychotics lower seizure threshold, prolong QT

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration, dysrhythmias, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis; excessive sedation → respiratory depression
Malnutrition → Wernicke encephalopathy: confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia; suspected → high-dose IV thiamine
Pregnancy: seizures, adrenergic surge → fetal hypoxia; **maternal withdrawal** is greatest immediate fetal risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: High-risk inpatients → preventive benzodiazepines; outpatient withdrawal only if mild, reliable supervision
Recovery: **naltrexone** unless opioids/acute hepatitis; **acamprosate** unless severe CKD; addiction follow-up

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hepatic encephalopathy: asterixis, decompensated cirrhosis, less autonomic excitation
Sepsis: infectious source, hypotension, persistent inflammatory findings
Sedative withdrawal: benzodiazepine/barbiturate reduction; similar syndrome, different exposure
Anticholinergic delirium: dry skin, urinary retention; diaphoresis favors withdrawal

table.title: Approximate onset after reduction; overlap common
rows: Visual/auditory/tactile hallucinations; clear sensorium; vitals near normal
Disorientation, hallucinations, fever, tremor, marked autonomic instability

amniotic-fluid-embolism.name: Amniotic fluid embolism
amniotic-fluid-embolism.scope: Cardiogenic shock, respiratory failure, acute hypoxemia, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), massive transfusion protocol, supportive critical care
amniotic-fluid-embolism.core: Abrupt hypoxemia, cardiovascular collapse, and DIC during labor or shortly after delivery suggest amniotic fluid embolism.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Labor, cesarean/vaginal delivery, placental disruption; unpredictable and usually unpreventable
Reported associations: advanced maternal age, abnormal placentation, induction; associations do not establish causation

rows.label: Clues
items: Sudden dyspnea, cyanosis, agitation, seizure, profound hypotension, fetal bradycardia
★ **Bleeding from IV sites or uterine hemorrhage** with falling fibrinogen suggests consumptive coagulopathy
May present chiefly as coagulopathy; absence of the full triad early does not exclude disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Maternal inflammatory response to amniotic components triggers pulmonary vasoconstriction and coagulation activation
Acute right ventricular failure may progress to left ventricular dysfunction and pulmonary edema

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis of exclusion**; no definitive blood test or imaging marker
ABG, CBC, PT/aPTT, fibrinogen, crossmatch; bedside echocardiography helps characterize shock
Fetal squamous cells in pulmonary circulation are neither necessary nor specific
Exclude hemorrhage, pulmonary thromboembolism, anaphylaxis, high neuraxial block, eclampsia without delaying resuscitation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **High-quality CPR**, left uterine displacement, oxygenation/intubation; activate obstetric/anesthesia/critical-care teams
Vasopressors/inotropes guided by echocardiography; avoid fluid overload with RV failure
★ **Massive transfusion protocol**: red cells, plasma, platelets; replace fibrinogen with cryoprecipitate/concentrate
Arrest, uterus ≥umbilicus, no ROSC → resuscitative delivery: start by 4 minutes, birth by 5
Operate at arrest location without transport delay; consider ECMO for refractory cardiopulmonary failure

rows.label: Complications
items: Hypoxic brain injury, multiorgan failure, exsanguination, maternal death; fetal hypoxic injury/death

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pulmonary embolism: thrombotic risk, RV strain; immediate profound DIC less characteristic
Anaphylaxis: trigger exposure, urticaria/bronchospasm; treat epinephrine
Hemorrhagic shock: bleeding precedes collapse, rather than unexplained respiratory failure first

amniotic-fluid-embolism.evidence: Resuscitation checked 2026-10-30: [SMFM updated AFE checklist, 2026](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13565333/); clinical patterns established teaching.

anaphylaxis.name: Anaphylaxis
anaphylaxis.scope: Anaphylaxis, angioedema, biphasic reactions, epinephrine autoinjector, emergency airway management
anaphylaxis.core: Rapid multisystem reaction after exposure—or isolated hypotension or airway compromise after a known allergen—requires epinephrine immediately.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Foods, insect venom, antibiotics, latex; exercise can amplify food-triggered reactions
Asthma, prior severe reaction, mast-cell disorders; beta-blockers can complicate treatment

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Urticaria/angioedema + wheeze, stridor, hypotension, or severe GI symptoms**
Skin findings may be absent; hoarseness and tongue swelling predict airway danger
Biphasic recurrence after apparent resolution, especially after severe or undertreated episodes

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Mast-cell/basophil mediators → vasodilation, capillary leak, bronchoconstriction; often IgE-mediated
Epinephrine: α1 reverses vasodilation/edema, β2 reverses bronchoconstriction; albuterol alone misses edema and shock

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; never wait for tryptase or laboratory confirmation
Acute and baseline serum tryptase can support uncertain cases; normal results do not exclude anaphylaxis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **IM epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg**, adult 0.3–0.5 mg, lateral thigh; repeat every 5–15 minutes
Supine with legs elevated unless respiratory distress; oxygen, early intubation for progressive obstruction
Profound shock or refractory hypotension → titrated IV epinephrine plus **isotonic boluses**; beta-blocker use → glucagon
Albuterol for residual bronchospasm; antihistamines relieve itching only; steroids do not reliably prevent biphasic reactions
★ Monitor until resolved; **longer observation/admission** after hypotension, repeated epinephrine, or severe asthma

rows.label: Complications
items: Asphyxia, distributive shock, arrhythmia, hypoxic brain injury
Undiluted IV epinephrine bolus errors → ischemia and dangerous dysrhythmia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Prescribe **epinephrine autoinjector**, demonstrate technique, provide written action plan and allergy referral
Extra device for repeat-dose risk; avoidance, medical alert ID; venom immunotherapy after qualifying sting allergy

rows.label: Mimics
items: Vasovagal episode: bradycardia, pallor, rapid improvement supine
Bradykinin angioedema: no itching/hives; ACE inhibitor or hereditary disease → airway, icatibant/C1 inhibitor

antepartum-bleeding.name: Antepartum bleeding
antepartum-bleeding.scope: Placenta previa, placental abruption, vasa previa, uterine rupture, transabdominal ultrasound before digital exam, Kleihauer-Betke test, emergent cesarean delivery
antepartum-bleeding.core: Bleeding in later pregnancy requires immediate maternal stabilization and fetal assessment, followed by placental localization before any digital cervical examination.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Previa: prior cesarean, multiparity; abruption: hypertension, cocaine, trauma, prior abruption
Vasa previa: velamentous cord, accessory placental lobe, IVF; rupture: uterine scar, obstructed labor

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Shock may exceed visible blood loss** with concealed abruption or internal hemorrhage
Assess uterine tone, pain, contractions, fetal tracing, membrane status; bleeding volume alone is unreliable

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Maternal placental bleeding versus fetal vessel hemorrhage; vasa previa can rapidly exsanguinate fetus
Placental separation or uterine disruption compromises oxygen delivery independent of maternal external blood loss

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ CBC, type/crossmatch, coagulation studies including fibrinogen; continuous fetal monitoring if viable
★ **Ultrasound before digital examination**; transabdominal first; transvaginal safely clarifies placenta–cervix relationship
Normal ultrasound does not exclude abruption; suspected rupture is a clinical emergency
Rh-negative bleeding/trauma → Kleihauer–Betke or flow cytometry quantifies fetomaternal hemorrhage for anti-D dosing

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ ABCs, two large IVs, blood products when needed; **do not delay delivery for imaging if unstable**
Hemorrhage/fetal compromise → emergency cesarean; rupture → laparotomy, uterine repair or hysterectomy
Stable preterm previa → observation, pelvic rest, corticosteroids when eligible; planned cesarean before labor
Abruption: deliver if significant or compromised; vaginal birth possible when stable and imminent or fetal demise
Unsensitized Rh-negative patient → anti-D immunoglobulin; correct abruption-associated coagulopathy

rows.label: Complications
items: Hemorrhagic shock, DIC, AKI, hysterectomy; fetal hypoxia, death, prematurity
Previa plus cesarean scar increases placenta accreta spectrum risk and operative hemorrhage

rows.label: Prevention
items: Control BP, avoid cocaine/tobacco; prenatal placental/cord localization and planned high-risk delivery

rows.label: Mimics
items: Bloody show: small mucus-streaked bleeding with cervical change
Cervical lesion: contact bleeding, visible source on speculum examination

table.title: Critical distinctions
rows: Bleeding after rupture; sudden fetal bradycardia
Scarred uterus; sudden pain, lost station, fetal bradycardia

antepartum-bleeding.evidence: Not checked online; established obstetric hemorrhage teaching.

antipsychotics.name: Antipsychotics
antipsychotics.scope: First-generation vs second-generation, extrapyramidal symptoms (acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia), neuroleptic malignant syndrome, metabolic syndrome, hyperprolactinemia, QTc prolongation
antipsychotics.core: Dopamine-modulating drugs treat psychosis and mania; selection depends on motor, metabolic, endocrine, cardiovascular, and hematologic risks.

rows.label: Use
items: ★ Psychosis, mania, agitation; **SGA first-line**; **clozapine** if resistant or recurrent suicidality
FGA: mainly D2 antagonism; SGA: D2/5-HT2 effects, varying by agent
Quetiapine sedation → switch to aripiprazole; obesity → ziprasidone, not olanzapine/clozapine

rows.label: Mechanism
items: Nigrostriatal blockade → movement disorders; tuberoinfundibular blockade → prolactin elevation
Aripiprazole: partial D2 agonist; haloperidol high-potency FGA, chlorpromazine low-potency FGA
Chronic D2 blockade → receptor supersensitivity → tardive dyskinesia; can worsen after stopping

rows.label: Adverse
items: ★ Fever, **lead-pipe rigidity**, autonomic instability, high CK → NMS; stop drug, supportive ICU care
Severe NMS: dantrolene/bromocriptine; olanzapine/clozapine: weight gain, diabetes, dyslipidemia
Risperidone: ↑prolactin; ziprasidone: ↑QT; clozapine: neutropenia, myocarditis, ileus, seizures

rows.label: Avoid
items: Lewy body/Parkinson disease: severe sensitivity; specialist-selected quetiapine/clozapine if essential
Dementia: ↑mortality, falls; dangerous behavior after safer measures → low-dose **quetiapine**/risperidone, not benzodiazepines

rows.label: Interactions
items: Other QT-prolonging drugs, electrolyte depletion → torsades; sedatives/alcohol increase CNS depression
Metoclopramide, prochlorperazine block dopamine: same EPS, tardive dyskinesia, NMS; avoid after NMS

rows.label: Monitor
items: ★ Weight/BMI, BP, glucose/A1c, lipids; movement examinations; **ANC with clozapine**
ECG for cardiac/QT risks; prolactin when symptomatic; ask about bowel function
Clozapine + ANC <1000 → **hold clozapine**, not dose reduction; ANC 1000–1499 → continue, closer monitoring

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Anticholinergics worsen tardive dyskinesia**; valbenazine/deutetrabenazine are VMAT2 inhibitors
Akathisia can mimic worsening agitation; increasing antipsychotic dose can worsen it
Low-potency FGAs: more orthostasis/anticholinergic effects; high-potency FGAs: more EPS

table.title: Extrapyramidal syndromes
rows: Stop/switch culprit first; benztropine or amantadine

antipsychotics.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [FDA clozapine monitoring update](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-and-availability/fda-removes-risk-evaluation-and-mitigation-strategy-rems-program-antipsychotic-drug-clozapine); other effects established teaching.

aortic-dissection.name: Aortic dissection
aortic-dissection.core: Sudden maximal chest or back pain with vascular or neurologic deficits suggests aortic dissection, even without widened mediastinum.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Long-standing hypertension → **medial degeneration** in older adults; bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation
Marfan/vascular Ehlers-Danlos, pregnancy, cocaine, aortic instrumentation or aneurysm

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Abrupt severe pain**, pulse/BP asymmetry, syncope, focal neurologic deficit
New aortic regurgitation murmur; limb ischemia or abdominal pain from branch-vessel malperfusion
Hypotension suggests rupture, tamponade, severe regurgitation, or coronary involvement

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Intimal tear → blood separates medial layers, creating false lumen
Propagation compromises branch arteries or ruptures into pericardium/pleura

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Stable → **CTA chest/abdomen/pelvis**; unstable or unable to leave resuscitation → bedside TEE
Chest radiograph may show widened mediastinum but normal film does not exclude dissection
ECG/troponin may mimic MI; high suspicion requires aortic imaging before antithrombotics
Examine bilateral arm pressures, femoral pulses, neurologic status, renal function

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **IV esmolol or labetalol** + opioid analgesia; target HR 60–80 and SBP <120 if perfusion maintained
Persistent hypertension after rate control → nicardipine or nitroprusside; avoid vasodilator before beta blockade
★ **Avoid anticoagulation and thrombolysis** when dissection suspected
Tamponade from dissection → immediate surgical team; routine pericardiocentesis can worsen hemorrhage

rows.label: Complications
items: Aortic rupture, hemothorax, tamponade, MI, stroke, paraplegia, mesenteric/renal ischemia
Late aneurysmal dilation or recurrent dissection despite initial successful treatment

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Lifelong **BP control and surveillance CTA/MRA**; beta-blocker-based regimen
Avoid heavy isometric lifting; screen first-degree relatives for familial aortopathy

rows.label: Mimics
items: Acute coronary syndrome: pressure-like pain, no pulse deficit; coexistence possible
PE: pleuritic pain, hypoxemia, right-heart strain
Esophageal rupture: vomiting followed by pain and subcutaneous emphysema

aortic-dissection.evidence: Not checked online; established aortic emergency principles.

asthma.name: Asthma
asthma.scope: Diagnosis, stepwise therapy, acute exacerbation, exercise-induced bronchoconstriction
asthma.core: Variable episodes of wheeze, cough, dyspnea, and chest tightness from reversible expiratory airflow limitation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: **Family history of asthma/atopy**: strongest childhood risk; allergens, viral infections, smoke, occupational sensitizers
Exercise/cold air, aspirin-sensitive disease, nonselective beta-blockers; assess workplace symptom pattern

rows.label: Clues
items: Nocturnal/early-morning symptoms; normal examination between attacks
★ **Silent chest, exhaustion, altered mentation, rising PaCO2** → impending respiratory failure
Acute attack: low peak flow, accessory-muscle use, difficulty speaking
Cough-variant: isolated chronic cough, worse with cold/exercise; normal examination and radiograph

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Allergen cross-links IgE on **mast cells** → histamine, leukotrienes → bronchoconstriction
Airway inflammation, smooth-muscle constriction, mucus → variable obstruction and hyperresponsiveness
Persistent uncontrolled inflammation → remodeling with incompletely reversible airflow limitation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Spirometry**: obstruction with bronchodilator FEV1 increase >12% and >200 mL in adults
Normal spirometry with suspicion → repeat during symptoms or methacholine challenge
Exercise challenge: postexercise FEV1 fall >10%; assess baseline control before isolated exercise diagnosis
PFT pattern: ↓FEV1, normal/↓FVC, normal/↑TLC from air trapping

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Exacerbation → **repeated inhaled albuterol + ipratropium**, oxygen, early systemic glucocorticoids
Severe poor response → IV magnesium; deterioration → intubation; avoid sedatives and routine antibiotics
Exercise symptoms → preexercise albuterol or prescribed ICS-formoterol; persistent symptoms → improve controller
Check technique/adherence before stepping up; uncontrolled despite high-dose ICS-LABA → phenotype-directed biologic referral
Discharge: **PEF ≥70–80% predicted** (less wheeze is unreliable) + 5–7 day **oral prednisone** prevents relapse

rows.label: Complications
items: Status asthmaticus, pneumothorax, respiratory arrest
ICS → thrush/dysphonia; systemic steroids → osteoporosis, hyperglycemia, adrenal suppression

rows.label: Prevention
items: Written action plan, trigger reduction, smoking cessation, spacer; rinse mouth after ICS
★ GINA: **no SABA-only treatment**, no LABA monotherapy; ICS with every reliever use
Older exam questions (NAEPP) may expect: symptoms ≤2 days/week, awakenings ≤2/month → **SABA alone**; more → daily ICS

rows.label: Mimics
items: Inducible laryngeal obstruction: inspiratory stridor, inspiratory flow-loop flattening
COPD: persistent obstruction, smoking history
HF: edema, elevated JVP, cardiac findings
Deconditioning: obese/sedentary, exertional dyspnea; normal PFTs, no bronchodilator response

atopic-dermatitis.name: Atopic dermatitis
atopic-dermatitis.scope: Atopic dermatitis, pruritus, flexural lichenification, emollients and topical corticosteroids, complications (eczema herpeticum, bacterial infection)
atopic-dermatitis.core: Chronic relapsing itchy eczema with xerosis; infants often have facial/extensor disease, while older children develop flexural lichenification.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Personal/family atopy, impaired skin barrier, dry climate; soaps, wool, fragrances, heat can trigger flares
Asthma and allergic rhinitis commonly coexist; scratching and bacterial colonization exacerbate inflammation

rows.label: Clues
items: Excoriations, erythema, oozing during flares; sleep disturbance and chronic thickening from rubbing
★ **Painful monomorphic punched-out erosions**, fever, rapid spread → eczema herpeticum
Honey-colored crusts, pustules, warmth or spreading erythema → secondary bacterial infection

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Barrier dysfunction increases water loss and allergen penetration; type 2 inflammation drives itch–scratch cycle

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis** by itch, distribution, chronicity; no routine serum IgE/food allergy panels
Atypical/refractory disease → assess contact allergy, infestation, immune deficiency; selected patch testing
Suspected HSV complication → lesion PCR, but begin treatment before results if clinically convincing

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Daily **thick emollient**, short lukewarm bathing, fragrance-free cleanser; apply moisturizer promptly afterward
★ Flares → **topical corticosteroid**, potency by site/severity: triamcinolone on body; hydrocortisone on face/folds
Tacrolimus/pimecrolimus for sensitive sites or steroid-sparing maintenance; wet wraps for selected severe flares
Refractory moderate/severe disease → phototherapy or dupilumab; avoid chronic systemic glucocorticoids
★ Eczema herpeticum → **systemic acyclovir** now; ocular involvement → ophthalmology

rows.label: Complications
items: S aureus superinfection, disseminated HSV, sleep loss, psychosocial burden
Excess topical steroid potency/duration → skin atrophy, striae; dupilumab → conjunctivitis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Barrier care, trigger reduction, short nails; intermittent maintenance anti-inflammatory treatment at recurrent sites
No empiric elimination diets without confirmed clinical allergy; avoid routine antibiotics for uninfected eczema

rows.label: Mimics
items: Contact dermatitis: exposure-shaped distribution, patch-test association
Scabies: nocturnal household itch, burrows in webs/wrists
Seborrheic dermatitis: greasy scale, less itching

attention-deficit-hyperactivity-disorder.name: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder
attention-deficit-hyperactivity-disorder.scope: Diagnostic criteria across two settings, behavioral rating scales from parents and teachers, behavioral therapy, stimulant pharmacotherapy
attention-deficit-hyperactivity-disorder.core: Persistent developmentally inappropriate inattention and/or hyperactivity–impulsivity causing functional impairment across settings, with childhood onset.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Strong genetic contribution, prematurity, prenatal tobacco/alcohol exposure; symptoms may persist into adulthood
Learning disorders, anxiety, oppositional behavior, sleep problems and substance use commonly coexist

rows.label: Clues
items: Inattention: lost items, distraction, disorganization; hyperactivity: fidgeting, leaving seat, excessive talking
Impulsivity: interrupting, difficulty waiting; presentations can be inattentive, hyperactive–impulsive, or combined
Academic difficulty alone insufficient; assess family, peer, driving, and workplace function

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Altered dopamine/norepinephrine executive-control signaling; inconsistent performance does not imply deliberate behavior

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **≥6 symptoms per domain**, or ≥5 if age ≥17; duration ≥6 months
★ Several symptoms **before age 12**, present in ≥2 settings, with impairment; exclude better explanations
Parent and teacher DSM-based rating scales, such as Vanderbilt; interview child and evaluate comorbidities
Check vision/hearing, sleep, learning needs; no routine EEG, neuroimaging, or laboratory diagnostic test

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Ages 4–5: **parent-training behavioral management** first; methylphenidate for persistent moderate/severe impairment
★ Age ≥6: **methylphenidate or amphetamine** plus behavioral/classroom intervention and educational supports
Atomoxetine, extended-release guanfacine/clonidine when stimulants unsuitable, ineffective, or diversion concerning
Before prescribing: personal/family cardiac history, BP/HR, height/weight; ECG only if cardiac concern
Titrate to function and adverse effects; monitor appetite, sleep, growth, BP, misuse; reassess across settings

rows.label: Complications
items: Injury, academic failure, relationship problems; untreated impairment increases later substance-use risk
Stimulants → appetite suppression, insomnia, tachycardia; atomoxetine → suicidality warning, rare liver injury

rows.label: Prevention
items: Routines, sleep, positive reinforcement, school accommodations; secure medication against diversion

rows.label: Mimics
items: Absence seizures: brief stereotyped unresponsiveness with abrupt recovery
Anxiety: attention disrupted by worry
Sleep apnea: snoring, poor sleep, daytime behavioral dysfunction

bartholin-gland-cyst-and-abscess.name: Bartholin gland cyst and abscess
bartholin-gland-cyst-and-abscess.scope: Asymptomatic cyst, symptomatic cyst, acute Bartholin abscess, incision and drainage, Word catheter placement, marsupialization, excision for recurrent or older women
bartholin-gland-cyst-and-abscess.core: Obstructed posterior vestibular gland causing a cyst or abscess; durable drainage prevents recurrence, and age determines the need for malignancy assessment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Reproductive age, prior duct obstruction, previous cyst/abscess; usually polymicrobial vaginal/enteric flora
STIs may coexist but most abscesses are not solely gonococcal or chlamydial

rows.label: Clues
items: Cyst: soft fluctuant, often painless; abscess: marked tenderness, erythema, difficulty sitting/walking
Gland location near 4 or 8 o'clock at vaginal opening; usually unilateral
Firm, fixed, irregular, recurrent, or postmenopausal lesion → malignancy concern

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Duct occlusion retains gland secretions; bacterial infection produces purulence
Drainage without an epithelialized outlet allows rapid closure and recurrence

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical vulvar examination**; assess cellulitis, systemic illness, pregnancy, immune status
GC/chlamydia NAAT when sexual risk or cervicitis; culture selected recurrent/severe infections
★ **Biopsy at age ≥40 or suspicious mass**; imaging unnecessary for typical superficial lesion

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Management branches below; **Word catheter about 4 weeks** permits an epithelialized drainage tract
★ Avoid **incision alone or needle aspiration**: rapid closure causes recurrence
Antibiotics only for cellulitis, systemic infection, immunocompromise, or confirmed STI; uncomplicated drainage needs none
Persistent recurrence → gland excision after acute inflammation settles

rows.label: Complications
items: Recurrent abscess, surrounding cellulitis, rare sepsis; early catheter expulsion can compromise tract formation
Excision → bleeding, scarring, dyspareunia; older patients risk missed gland malignancy

rows.label: Prevention
items: Complete catheter follow-up, hygiene without irritating products; condoms/STI treatment for exposure-related infection
No proven universal prevention of duct obstruction; return promptly for recurrent pain, fever, or mass

rows.label: Mimics
items: Skene duct cyst: periurethral/anterior location
Epidermal inclusion cyst: superficial skin nodule, possible punctum
Hidradenitis: recurrent multiple intertriginous nodules, sinus tracts

bartholin-gland-cyst-and-abscess.evidence: Not checked online; established gynecologic office-procedure teaching.

benign-breast-conditions.name: Benign breast conditions
benign-breast-conditions.scope: Fibroadenoma, fibrocystic changes, intraductal papilloma, breast cyst, fat necrosis, galactocele, breast abscess
benign-breast-conditions.core: Breast symptoms require age-directed imaging and clinical–radiologic concordance; a benign-appearing examination alone cannot exclude malignancy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Reproductive hormonal cycling; milk stasis; breast trauma or prior surgery
Smoking predisposes to recurrent subareolar abscess
**Cracked, excoriated nipples** → main portal of entry for lactational mastitis

rows.label: Clues
items: Galactocele: cystic lactational/postlactational mass, no inflammation, varies with feeds; fat–fluid level on imaging
Mastitis: focal tender erythema, fever, no fluctuance; abscess adds **fluctuance**; often Staphylococcus aureus
★ Spontaneous unilateral **bloody single-duct discharge** → usually **papilloma**; exclude malignancy, persistent → surgical evaluation
Nonbloody discharge only on expression, normal exam → **physiologic**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Hormone-responsive stromal/glandular tissue produces cyclic changes; duct obstruction causes retained secretions
Adipose injury causes inflammatory necrosis and calcification that can resemble cancer

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Palpable mass **<30 years → ultrasound**; ≥30 → diagnostic mammography with targeted ultrasound
Suspicious solid lesion or imaging–exam discordance → **core needle biopsy**
Simple cyst: anechoic, thin-walled, posterior enhancement; no solid component
Nonlactational abscess or persistent inflammation after antibiotics → exclude underlying carcinoma
Cyclic bilateral nodularity, no dominant mass → **reexamine after menses**, before imaging

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Painful simple cyst → aspiration; nonbloody fluid + full collapse → benign; bloody fluid/residual mass → **biopsy**
Fibroadenoma → observe when concordant; excise if rapidly enlarging, large or symptomatic
Breast pain, no mass, young, normal exam → **reassurance**; fibrocystic pain → supportive bra, topical/oral NSAID
★ Mastitis → **dicloxacillin/cephalexin**, keep breastfeeding/pumping; abscess → add needle/incision drainage; MRSA → clindamycin
Tender lactating lump, no erythema/fever → **warm compresses**, keep nursing; persistent galactocele → aspiration

rows.label: Complications
items: Recurrent periductal abscess → fistula; incomplete drainage → persistent infection
Proliferative lesions with atypia increase future cancer risk; simple cysts do not

rows.label: Prevention
items: Effective breast emptying during lactation; smoking cessation for recurrent periductal disease

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cancer: irregular fixed mass, retraction or suspicious nodes
Phyllodes: rapidly enlarging fibroepithelial mass requiring excision

table.title: Common benign findings
rows: Early postpartum; bilateral tense tender breasts, low fever

benign-breast-conditions.evidence: Not checked online; established breast diagnostic principles.

bipolar-disorder.name: Bipolar disorder
bipolar-disorder.scope: Bipolar I (manic episode, DIG FAST), bipolar II (hypomania and major depression), cyclothymic disorder, acute mania pharmacotherapy (antipsychotics, lithium, valproate), maintenance therapy
bipolar-disorder.core: Distinct episodes of pathologically increased energy with elevated or irritable mood distinguish bipolar illness from ordinary mood variability.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Strong family history; typical onset adolescence/young adulthood
Sleep deprivation, antidepressants, stimulants, substances can precipitate episodes

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **DIG FAST**: distractibility, impulsivity, grandiosity, flight of ideas, activity, decreased sleep need, talkativeness
≥3 associated symptoms; ≥4 if mood only irritable
Mania: psychosis, marked impairment, risky spending/sex, or hospitalization; reduced sleep without fatigue

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Multifactorial genetic vulnerability with dysregulated mood, reward and circadian systems

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical longitudinal history + collateral**; ask about prior elevated episodes before treating depression
Assess suicidality, pregnancy, substance use; TSH, metabolic panel, toxicology to exclude secondary causes
Hospitalization requirement can establish manic duration criterion even before one week
Major depression ≥2 weeks; hypomania causes no psychosis, marked impairment or hospitalization
Cyclothymia: symptoms ≥half the time; no symptom-free interval >2 months or full mood episodes

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute mania → **antipsychotic** (olanzapine/quetiapine); severe → add lithium/valproate; mixed/rapid cycling → **divalproex**
Unsafe, psychotic, severely agitated, or unable to care for self → hospitalization
Depression → quetiapine, lurasidone, lithium, lamotrigine; urgent/refractory or first-trimester psychotic mania → **ECT**
★ **Avoid antidepressant monotherapy**; lamotrigine does not treat acute mania
Maintenance: lithium, quetiapine, valproate or lamotrigine selected by episode pattern; lithium reduces suicide risk

rows.label: Complications
items: Suicide, substance misuse, financial/relationship loss; metabolic adverse effects of antipsychotics
Lithium: renal/thyroid toxicity; valproate/carbamazepine: teratogenicity, avoid in first trimester; lamotrigine: severe rash

rows.label: Prevention
items: Regular sleep, psychoeducation, relapse-sign monitoring, maintenance adherence; avoid stimulants and substance misuse

rows.label: Mimics
items: ADHD: chronic baseline symptoms rather than distinct mood episodes
Borderline personality: brief reactive shifts linked to interpersonal stress
Medication/substance-induced mania: onset after antidepressant, stimulant, steroid → **stop culprit first**
Hyperthyroidism: heat intolerance, tremor, low TSH

table.title: Diagnostic branches
rows: Hypomania ≥4 days + major depression; never mania

bowel-obstruction.name: Bowel obstruction
bowel-obstruction.scope: Small bowel obstruction (adhesions, hernia), large bowel obstruction (volvulus, malignancy), paralytic ileus, NG decompression, surgical management
bowel-obstruction.core: Colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, distention, and obstipation suggest mechanical obstruction; constant pain or systemic toxicity raises concern for strangulation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior abdominal surgery (**adhesions**, leading cause), incarcerated hernia, Crohn strictures → small-bowel obstruction
Colorectal malignancy, chronic constipation, institutionalization → large-bowel obstruction or sigmoid volvulus
Recent surgery, opioids, hypokalemia, severe systemic illness → ileus

rows.label: Clues
items: Early high-pitched sounds may become absent; proximal obstruction causes earlier vomiting, distal disease greater distention
★ **Peritonitis, fever, tachycardia, rising lactate**, or continuous severe pain → ischemia/perforation
Complete → **obstipation**, no flatus; partial may still pass stool/diarrhea, not excluding obstruction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Luminal blockage → upstream dilation, third spacing; closed loop compromises venous then arterial supply
Adynamic ileus reflects impaired motility without an anatomic transition point

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast** defines transition point, cause, and ischemic signs
CBC, electrolytes, creatinine, lactate; normal lactate cannot exclude early ischemia
Radiograph may show dilated loops/air-fluid levels, no rectal gas; CT more definitive if diagnosis uncertain
★ Massive colonic distention + **coffee-bean (inverted-U) loop** on radiograph → sigmoid volvulus
Pregnancy: plain radiograph acceptable first (minimal fetal dose); MRI if unclear; do not delay

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **NPO, IV isotonic fluids, electrolyte correction**; NG decompression for significant vomiting/distention
★ Strangulation, perforation, closed loop, or incarcerated hernia → **urgent surgery** + ceftriaxone/metronidazole
Uncomplicated adhesive SBO → surgical observation, serial examination; water-soluble contrast helps predict resolution
Failure to improve during a short monitored trial, commonly up to 72 h → operation
Ileus → correct trigger, reduce opioids, mobilize; no operation solely for absent sounds

rows.label: Complications
items: Dehydration, AKI, hypokalemic alkalosis; bowel necrosis, perforation, sepsis
Recurrent adhesions; short-bowel syndrome after extensive resection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early postoperative ambulation, opioid-sparing analgesia, electrolyte correction; elective repair of symptomatic hernias

rows.label: Mimics
items: Gastroenteritis: prominent diarrhea, no focal transition point
Mesenteric ischemia: pain out of proportion before peritoneal signs
Ileus: hypoactive/absent sounds, gas throughout bowel including rectum
Diabetic autonomic neuropathy: dysmotility, dilated loops without transition point

table.title: Large-bowel branches
rows: Sigmoidoscopic detorsion, rectal tube → same-admission resection

bowel-obstruction.evidence: Not checked online; established acute surgical management principles.

brain-death.name: Brain death
brain-death.scope: Prerequisites (normothermia, normal BP), clinical exam (coma, absent brainstem reflexes), apnea test, ancillary testing (cerebral blood flow studies)
brain-death.core: Permanent loss of all brain function, including brainstem function, constitutes death; a beating heart on ventilation does not negate the diagnosis.

rows.label: Principle
items: Known catastrophic irreversible brain injury; compatible neuroimaging; adequate observation period
No family consent needed; after declaration → stop ventilator, unless organ donation planned

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Prerequisites: **temperature ≥36°C**, adult SBP ≥100 and MAP ≥75 mm Hg
Exclude paralysis/metabolic confounders; sedatives: ≥5 half-lives, longer if impaired clearance
★ Examination: **coma**, no brain-mediated motor response; absent brainstem reflexes (table)

rows.label: Don't
items: Oculocephalic testing with possible cervical injury; use caloric testing after confirming ear integrity
Declare death with any brain-mediated response or spontaneous breath
Use ancillary testing to bypass hypothermia or high CNS-depressant levels

rows.label: Exceptions
items: Spinal reflex movements may persist without contradicting diagnosis
Incomplete examination or unsafe apnea test → radionuclide cerebral perfusion or catheter angiography
After temperature ≤35.5°C, wait ≥24 hours following rewarming to ≥36°C

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Apnea test: no breaths, **PaCO2 ≥60 and ≥20 above baseline**, pH <7.30
Preoxygenate; abort apnea testing for hypotension, hypoxemia or unstable arrhythmia
★ 2023 update: **EEG no longer accepted** as ancillary testing; pediatric requirements differ

cervicitis-pid.name: Cervicitis and pelvic inflammatory disease
cervicitis-pid.core: Sexually active patient with mucopurulent discharge or postcoital bleeding; ascending infection adds pelvic pain, sometimes an adnexal abscess.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age <25 (adolescent cervical ectopy → vulnerable columnar epithelium), new/multiple partners, inconsistent condoms, prior STI
IUD-associated PID risk concentrated within first 3 weeks after insertion

rows.label: Clues
items: Cervical friability, easily induced endocervical bleeding; infection sometimes asymptomatic
Dyspareunia, fever; severe unilateral pain/adnexal mass → **tubo-ovarian abscess**
Peritonitis, shock → rupture; RUQ pain → Fitz-Hugh–Curtis perihepatitis
Persistent dysuria, sterile pyuria, negative culture → chlamydial urethritis, not UTI

rows.label: Pathophys
items: GC/CT ascend cervix → endometrium/tubes; PID often polymicrobial, including anaerobes
Chlamydial tubal damage: **host immune response** → scarring, hydrosalpinx

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Pregnancy test** first; vaginal/cervical or urine **GC/CT NAAT**; HIV/syphilis testing
★ Pelvic pain + **cervical motion, uterine, OR adnexal tenderness** → presumptive PID; no confirmation delay
Negative cervical NAAT does not exclude upper-tract infection; normal discharge/no vaginal leukocytes argues against PID
**Transvaginal US** for abscess or diagnostic uncertainty; routine laparoscopy unnecessary

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Cervicitis: empiric GC/CT coverage IF high risk/unreliable follow-up; otherwise await NAAT
★ Admit IF **pregnant, abscess, severe illness**, oral intolerance, uncertain surgical diagnosis, or failure by 72 h
Abscess rupture → emergency surgery; persistent abscess after 48–72 h antibiotics → drainage
Pregnant chlamydia → **azithromycin**, avoid doxycycline; retain IUD initially, reassess if no improvement

rows.label: Complications
items: Tubal infertility, ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain; abscess → sepsis

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Treat partners from prior **60 days**; abstain until courses completed, partners treated, symptoms resolved
Retest GC/CT at 3 months; pregnant chlamydia → test of cure at 4 weeks
Annual GC/CT screening: sexually active women <25, older women with risks; condoms

rows.label: Mimics
items: Ectopic pregnancy: positive hCG, no confirmed intrauterine pregnancy
Ovarian torsion: abrupt unilateral pain, vomiting; Doppler flow may persist
Appendicitis: migrating RLQ pain, CT appendiceal inflammation

table.title: Antibiotic branches
rows: Ceftriaxone; add CT regimen unless excluded
Oral drugs 14 days; ceftriaxone once IM outpatient

chancroid.name: Chancroid
chancroid.scope: Haemophilus ducreyi, painful genital ulcers with ragged undermined margins, painful fluctuant inguinal lymphadenitis (bubo), azithromycin, ceftriaxone, differentiation from syphilis and herpes
chancroid.core: Painful, friable genital ulcers with ragged undermined edges and tender suppurative inguinal nodes suggest Haemophilus ducreyi infection.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Sexual exposure in endemic regions/outbreaks, multiple partners, inconsistent condom use
HIV and lack of circumcision associated with slower healing and treatment failure

rows.label: Clues
items: Nonindurated ulcer base, purulent exudate, easy contact bleeding; often multiple lesions
Buboes commonly unilateral; lymph-node suppuration may cause draining sinus tracts
Systemic symptoms usually limited; generalized rash or neurologic findings suggest another infection

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Gram-negative coccobacillus enters mucosal breaks, producing local necrosis and regional lymphatic infection
Ulceration increases HIV acquisition and transmission risk

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Clinical suspicion plus exclusion of **syphilis and HSV**; test all genital ulcers
Ulcer HSV NAAT and syphilis serology; very early negative syphilis result requires repeat testing
H. ducreyi culture needs special media, limited sensitivity; NAAT availability limited
★ Obtain **HIV test**; consider repeat testing/PrEP according to ongoing exposure risk

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Azithromycin orally once** or **ceftriaxone IM once**
Fluctuant buboes → needle aspiration or incision/drainage plus antibiotics
★ Reexamine in **3–7 days**; symptoms should improve before complete ulcer healing
No response → reassess diagnosis, adherence, coinfection, HIV, or antimicrobial resistance

rows.label: Complications
items: Genital scarring, phimosis, fistulas, secondary infection; prolonged open lesions facilitate HIV spread

rows.label: Prevention
items: Condoms, abstain until lesions healed and partners treated
Examine/treat partners exposed during 10 days before symptom onset, even without symptoms

rows.label: Mimics
items: Syphilis: classically painless, indurated chancre with nontender nodes
HSV: grouped vesicles evolve into shallow ulcers; burning prodrome, recurrent episodes
LGV: small transient often painless lesion, later inguinal adenopathy or proctitis

colorectal-carcinoma.name: Colorectal carcinoma
colorectal-carcinoma.scope: Colon adenocarcinoma, rectal cancer, staging, surgical resection (hemicolectomy), liver metastases, chemotherapy
colorectal-carcinoma.core: Occult blood loss, altered bowel habits, or obstruction warrants colon evaluation; cancer stage determines local and systemic treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age, adenomas, Lynch/FAP, longstanding colitis, family history; smoking, obesity, processed meat

rows.label: Clues
items: Right-sided lesions → iron-deficiency anemia, fatigue, occult bleeding
Left-sided lesions → constipation, narrowed stools, obstruction; rectal lesions → tenesmus/hematochezia
Weight loss, palpable mass; hepatomegaly or elevated ALP suggests hepatic spread
Bladder invasion → colovesical fistula: fecaluria, mixed fecal flora in urine

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Adenoma–carcinoma sequence involves APC, KRAS, p53; mismatch-repair failure drives microsatellite instability
Portal drainage favors liver metastases; distal rectal tumors may spread directly to lungs

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Colonoscopy with biopsy**; evaluate entire colon for synchronous tumors
★ Confirmed cancer → **CT chest/abdomen/pelvis**, baseline CEA, tumor mismatch-repair/MSI testing
Rectal cancer → pelvic MRI for local staging; CEA cannot diagnose or screen
Obstruction/perforation → urgent contrast CT and surgical assessment

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Resectable colon cancer → **segmental colectomy with lymphadenectomy**; selected liver metastases → resection
Stage III → adjuvant FOLFOX/CAPOX; selected high-risk stage II → individualized chemotherapy
Locally advanced rectal cancer → neoadjuvant systemic chemotherapy/chemoradiation, then total mesorectal excision
Unresectable metastases, nonobstructing primary → **chemotherapy**, no primary resection; MSI-high → checkpoint inhibitor
Perforation or unstable obstruction → urgent operation; selected stable obstruction → stent or diversion

rows.label: Complications
items: Bleeding, perforation, malignant obstruction; venous thrombosis; oxaliplatin neuropathy
Postoperative anastomotic leak; pelvic treatment → urinary/sexual dysfunction

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Average-risk screening **45–75 years**; earlier colonoscopy for strong family history/hereditary syndromes
Postresection colonoscopy, CEA and stage-based CT surveillance; remove premalignant polyps

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hemorrhoids: outlet bleeding without explanatory anemia; do not dismiss alarm features
IBD: chronic inflammatory diarrhea; diverticulitis: acute focal pain and fever

colorectal-carcinoma.evidence: Screening checked 2026-10-30: [USPSTF colorectal screening](https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/colorectal-cancer-screening); treatment: established oncology teaching.

table.title: TNM essentials
rows: Extension through muscle; no regional nodal spread

congenital-heart-disease.name: Congenital heart disease
congenital-heart-disease.scope: Cyanotic heart disease (5 Ts: Tetralogy of Fallot, TGA, truncus, tricuspid atresia, TAPVR), acyanotic heart disease (VSD, ASD, PDA, coarctation of aorta), hyperoxia test, prostaglandin E1
congenital-heart-disease.core: Neonatal cyanosis or shock as the ductus closes demands urgent assessment for duct-dependent congenital heart disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Maternal diabetes, congenital rubella, family history; Down syndrome → AV septal defects
Prematurity → PDA; Turner syndrome → coarctation

rows.label: Clues
items: Poor feeding, diaphoresis, tachypnea, hepatomegaly → infant heart failure
